summary: This standards-track memo updates and extends the Policy Core LDAP schema from RFC 3703, based on the model extensions in RFC 3460. It adds new object classes and attributes so network policies can be stored in a directory.

plainLanguage.summary: Network rules can be stored in a directory like entries in a filing cabinet. This document adds more drawers and labels for them.

questions: how are network policies stored in ldap
subtitle: How network policy rules, conditions and actions from the extended policy model are stored as entries in an LDAP directory.

tldr.problem: The policy information model was extended by RFC 3460 with policy sets, compound conditions and actions, variables, values and filters, but the earlier LDAP schema in RFC 3703 could not store these new concepts.
tldr.mechanism: PCELS defines new LDAP object classes and attribute types, all prefixed pcels, that map each extended-model class to directory entries. Associations are realized through DN references, DIT containment, auxiliary class attachment or association entries.
tldr.outcome: A directory can hold nested, prioritized and reusable policies. It is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3703 and coexists with the older schema rather than replacing it.

today: RFC 4104 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2005 that updates RFC 3703, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC says it does not obsolete or deprecate the older schema, so both can coexist.

sections.title: Purpose and Place in the Policy Family
sections.content:
This document changes and extends the Policy Core LDAP Schema (PCLS, RFC 3703) to follow the model extensions of the Policy Core Information Model (PCIM) Extensions (RFC 3460). It consists of new LDAP object classes and attribute types. Some re-implement existing concepts under their new semantics from RFC 3460, and others implement concepts that RFC 3703 never covered. The RFC calls the result PCELS, the Policy Core Extension LDAP Schema.

It also adds two classes that do not come from RFC 3460, pcelsVendorVariableAuxClass and pcelsVendorValueAuxClass, as an extension mechanism for vendor-specific variables and values.

Three documents are prerequisites for reading it: the original model (RFC 3060), the extensions (RFC 3460) and RFC 3703. Mappings of the same model to other storage or transport technologies may be produced separately.
sections.plainLanguage: There was already a filing system for network rules. The rule makers invented new kinds of rules, so this document adds new folders to the same cabinet.

sections.title: The Class Hierarchy
sections.content:
All class and attribute names defined here start with pcels. Classes from PCLS start with pcim, classes from the DMTF CIM LDAP mapping start with dlm1, and top is the root of the LDAP schema. Figure 1 of the RFC shows the combined tree, marking each new class as abstract, auxiliary or structural.

The main new branches are:

  • pcelsPolicySet, with pcelsGroup and pcelsRule below it, each with an auxiliary and a structural form;
  • association classes for sets, conditions and actions;
  • condition and action auxiliary classes, simple and compound;
  • pcelsVariable and pcelsValueAuxClass with many subclasses for implicit variables and typed values;
  • reusable containers, role collections and device-level filter classes.

The pattern of an abstract base plus an auxiliary subclass (attach to an existing entry) and a structural subclass (a stand-alone entry) is used for groups, rules and reusable containers.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a family tree of folder types. The abstract ones are only blueprints, the auxiliary ones are stickers you put on an existing folder, and the structural ones are real folders.

sections.title: Mapping the Model to a Directory
sections.content:
The classes of the information model map directly to LDAP object classes and attribute types, with optimizations suited to a directory. An association in the model maps to one or more of four options: attributes that reference DNs (distinguished names), containment in the Directory Information Tree (DIT, superior-subordinate relationships), auxiliary class attachment, and association object classes with DN-referencing attributes. For example, a simple condition may be attached to a rule by attaching pcelsSimpleConditionAuxClass to a pcelsRuleInstance entry.

Two associations map to DIT containment. PolicyRoleCollectionInSystem is a weak association, and weak associations map well to containment. ReusablePolicy uses containment for scalability, because many policy instances are expected to sit in one reusable container.

Policy elements can be stored in two ways. A specific element belongs to the one rule or group that uses it and is contained under it. A reusable element lives in a reusable container and is reached by DN reference, so many policies can share it. Specific and reusable parts may be mixed in one policy set. The RFC walks through four cases of compound conditions combining specific or reusable compounds with specific or reusable components, and notes that the number of containers is chosen for administrative reasons with no effect on policy meaning.
sections.plainLanguage: A rule can keep its own private pieces in its own drawer, or it can point to shared pieces in a common drawer that many rules use.

sections.title: Policy Sets, Priorities and Strategies
sections.content:
The abstract class pcelsPolicySet represents a set of policies with a common decision strategy and a common set of roles. It is the parent of both groups and rules, so a rule can aggregate other rules or groups and nested structures can grow to any depth. Components are attached through pcelsPolicySetAssociation entries, which MUST carry a pcelsPriority attribute (a non-negative integer). Priority values MUST be unique among the associations directly under one set or system.

The pcelsDecisionStrategy attribute allows only 1 (FirstMatching) and 2 (AllMatching). If it is missing, applications MUST assume FirstMatching. The pcelsExecutionStrategy attribute on rules and compound actions allows 1 (Do until success), 2 (Do all) and 3 (Do until failure), with Do all assumed when it is missing. Policy roles continue to use the pcimRoles attribute from PCLS.

Because LDAP stores do not give a useful ordering of attribute values or search results, applications SHOULD sort components themselves after retrieval, using the pcelsPriority values. If a value violates its constraint, the entry SHOULD be treated as invalid and the rules or groups that refer to it SHOULD be treated as disabled.
sections.plainLanguage: Each rule in a set gets a ranking number, like a queue at school. The set also says whether to stop at the first rule that fits or to run every rule that fits.

sections.title: Conditions, Actions, Variables and Values
sections.content:
A rule's conditions and actions are tied to it by pcelsConditionAssociation and pcelsActionAssociation entries, listed through pcelsConditionList and pcelsActionList. The same mechanism lets a compound condition or compound action hold further conditions or actions. For a condition list, pcelsConditionListType allows 1 (Disjunctive) and 2 (Conjunctive), and disjunctive normal form is assumed when it is missing.

A simple condition or simple action combines one variable and one value. The variable is either attached to the same entry or referenced by DN through pcelsVariableDN, and likewise for pcelsValueDN. Attachment gives compact definitions that are efficient to fetch, while references allow reuse and administrative partitioning of the data.

Explicit variables name a CIM class property. Implicit variables have many subclasses for packet fields such as source and destination IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, ports, IP protocol and version, DSCP, source and destination MAC addresses and VLAN. Value classes cover IPv4, IPv6 and MAC addresses, strings, bit strings, integers and booleans. Device-level filter classes (pcelsIPHeadersFilter and pcels8021Filter) and pcelsFilterListAuxClass describe packet filters, and pcelsRoleCollection groups managed elements that share a role.
sections.plainLanguage: A simple condition is a question like "is the sender's address this one?". The variable is what you look at, and the value is what you compare it with.

sections.title: Coexistence with the Older Schema
sections.content:
PCELS does not obsolete or deprecate RFC 3703. The new items are defined to avoid interfering with a well-executed implementation of the older schema, and the intent is at least harmless coexistence of both models in one repository. Some PCLS classes (such as pcimPolicy, pcimRepository and the condition and action association and auxiliary classes) are used as parents, and if an application needs their function, implementations MUST also support them. Others, such as pcimRuleValidityAssociation, SHOULD be used when needed. Superseded ones, such as pcimRule and pcimGroup, MAY be supported.

When both exist, PCELS implementations SHOULD support the new schema and MAY also support the old one. The RFC lists changes that could affect older implementations: attributes such as pcimRoles are now also used by classes the older schema does not know, association classes are used through subclasses by pcelsRule, and repositories may contain entries of unknown types.
sections.plainLanguage: The old folders still work. New and old can sit in the same cabinet, but new systems should prefer the new folders.

sections.title: Vendor Extension Classes
sections.content: pcelsVendorVariableAuxClass and pcelsVendorValueAuxClass give a general way to represent policy variables and values that the model does not cover. Their properties define the content and format of the item. They are intended for vendor-specific extensions, and standardized extensions SHOULD NOT use them. The RFC adds that a particular submodel schema generally will not need them.
sections.plainLanguage: These are blank labels a company can use for its own special things that the standard list does not have.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The security considerations are those of the Policy Core LDAP Schema (RFC 3703). The RFC says the extensions add no further security considerations.

IANA registered the base object identifier 1.3.6.1.1.9 under the name pcelsSchema, and registered the LDAP descriptors for the new classes and attributes beneath it. For example, pcelsPolicySet is 1.3.6.1.1.9.1.1 and pcelsPolicySetName is 1.3.6.1.1.9.2.1.
sections.plainLanguage: The safety rules are the same as for the old cabinet, and every new folder type got an official number so no one else uses it.

items.title: DN references
items.text: An attribute holds the distinguished name of the related entry.

items.title: DIT containment
items.text: The related entry sits below the other in the directory tree.

items.title: Auxiliary class attachment
items.text: An auxiliary class is added to an existing entry.

items.title: Association classes
items.text: A separate entry type with attributes that reference DNs.

items.label: Do until success
items.desc: Actions are executed until one succeeds.

items.label: Do all
items.desc: All actions are executed. This is assumed when the attribute is missing.

items.label: Do until failure
items.desc: Actions are executed until one fails.
